Description: Seeking information that confirms your existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence. Most dangerous bias for founders — you'll only see what supports your idea.
Impact_On_Founders: Building product nobody wants because you ignored negative feedback. Hiring people who agree with you. Interpreting ambiguous data as positive.
Mitigation: Actively seek disconfirming evidence|Ask 'What would prove me wrong?'|Talk to people who DIDN'T buy|Red team your own assumptions|Use pre-mortem: 'If this fails, why?'

Description: Continuing to invest in something because you've already invested a lot — even when evidence says to stop. 'We've spent 6 months on this, we can't quit now.'
Impact_On_Founders: Refusing to pivot when data says product isn't working. Keeping bad hires because of training investment. Continuing features nobody uses.
Mitigation: Ask: 'If I started today with zero investment, would I still choose this?'|Set kill criteria BEFORE starting|Monthly 'continue/pivot/kill' review|Track investment vs outcome ratio

Description: Studying only successful startups and ignoring the thousands that failed doing the same thing. 'Dropbox succeeded with MVP, so I should too.'
Impact_On_Founders: Copying strategies from survivors without understanding the failures. Overestimating probability of success. Ignoring base rates (90% of startups fail).
Mitigation: Study FAILURES as much as successes|Ask 'How many tried this and failed?'|Look for base rates (what % succeed?)|Seek out post-mortem analyses|Remember: success stories are selection-biased

Description: Overestimating your ability in areas where you're actually a beginner. Then as you learn more, your confidence drops (the 'valley of despair').
Impact_On_Founders: First-time founders overconfident about market, product, and execution. Underestimating complexity of sales, marketing, legal. Not seeking expert help early enough.
Mitigation: Rate your confidence 1-10 in each domain|If >7 and no experience = likely DK effect|Hire advisors for low-competence areas|Embrace 'I don't know' as strength|Join founder peer groups for reality checks

Description: Feeling like a fraud despite evidence of competence. 75% of startup leaders experience it. Gets WORSE with success (more to lose).
Impact_On_Founders: Avoiding public speaking/PR, not raising prices, overworking to 'prove' yourself, not celebrating wins, comparing yourself to other founders constantly.
Mitigation: Recognize: 75% of founders feel this|Keep a 'wins' journal|Share feelings with founder peers|Reframe 'I don't know' as curiosity|Separate confidence from competence — you can be competent AND uncertain

Description: Quality of decisions degrades after making many decisions. Founders make 100+ decisions daily. By evening, you're making terrible choices.
Impact_On_Founders: Bad hiring decisions in afternoon interviews. Impulsive spending on tools. Saying yes to everything. Avoiding important decisions entirely.
Mitigation: Make important decisions in morning|Batch similar decisions|Create decision frameworks (pre-decide)|Reduce daily choices (clothes, meals, routines)|Delegate all decisions where you're not the bottleneck

Description: Break problems down to fundamental truths, then reason up from there. Opposite of reasoning by analogy ('everyone does it this way').
Impact_On_Founders: Building differentiated products by rethinking assumptions. Finding 10x cheaper solutions. Avoiding 'industry standard' traps.
Mitigation: Ask 'Why?' 5 times to reach fundamental truth|Question every assumption ('Is this actually true or just convention?')|Rebuild solution from base truths|Test: 'Would a smart person with no industry experience do it this way?'

Keywords: inversion,avoid failure,charlie munger,what not to do,pre-mortem
Description: Instead of 'How do I succeed?' ask 'How would I guarantee failure?' Then avoid those things. Charlie Munger: 'Invert, always invert.'
Impact_On_Founders: Identifying obvious failure modes: not talking to customers, building in isolation, ignoring finances, hiring wrong people, no legal structure.
Mitigation: Write down: '10 ways to guarantee my startup fails'|Are you doing ANY of these?|Pre-mortem before major decisions|Ask: 'What's the most likely way this goes wrong?'|Fix the avoidable failures first

Keywords: circle of competence,warren buffett,know what you know,expertise boundary
Description: Know where your expertise ends. Operate within your competence OR invest in learning. Warren Buffett: stay within your circle.
Impact_On_Founders: Making decisions in areas where you have no expertise (legal, accounting, technical architecture). Overextending into unfamiliar markets.
Mitigation: Map your circle: what do you GENUINELY know vs think you know?|Hire for gaps outside your circle|Be honest about blind spots|Expand circle deliberately through learning|Partner with people who have complementary circles

Description: Losses feel 2x more painful than equivalent gains feel good. Founders avoid risks that could produce big gains because of fear of loss.
Impact_On_Founders: Not raising prices (fear of losing customers). Not pivoting (fear of losing progress). Not firing underperformers (fear of conflict). Playing it safe when bold action is needed.
Mitigation: Reframe losses as learning investments|Calculate opportunity cost of NOT acting|Set loss limits upfront ('I'll try for 3 months, max $5K')|Ask: 'What's the cost of NOT doing this?'|Remember: biggest risk is often doing nothing
